conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Jordan, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the EPDS) to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the first year postpartum. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy—like music, a favorite show, or a cup of coffee—or has that pleasure slipped away?

I mean… I still try, but it’s like the spark isn’t really there. I’ll put on the show I used to love, and I’m half-watching while I nurse or fold laundry, but I don’t feel that little lift anymore. Same with coffee—my husband will hand me a hot cup and I drink it, but it just tastes… flat. I keep thinking, “I should be enjoying this,” and then I feel guilty for not even caring.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can laugh sometimes—like when the baby makes those funny faces while he’s sleeping—but it feels kind of forced. Mostly I’m too tired or worried to really find things funny. Even when my partner jokes around, I’ll smile, but the laughter doesn’t come as easily as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow we’ll go for a walk and it’ll feel nice,” but when the moment comes it just feels like another chore. Even simple stuff—like a friend texting to grab coffee—sounds exhausting instead of exciting. I still say yes sometimes, hoping the feeling will come back, but mostly I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I missed his sleepy cue or I’m not holding him the way he needs. When I spilled a little pumped milk last week, I sat on the kitchen floor and cried because it felt like I’d failed him. Even tiny stuff—dropping a burp cloth, forgetting to clip his nails—spirals into “I’m a terrible mom.” I know, rationally, accidents happen, but the voice in my head still says I should be better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down at night and my mind races with all these “what-ifs”—what if he rolls over in the crib, what if I sleep too hard and don’t hear him, what if I’m doing everything wrong. There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits in my chest like a weight. Sometimes I can talk myself down after a while, but it keeps popping back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It happens, yeah. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath, even when nothing’s happening. Last night I was just rocking the baby in the quiet living room and suddenly pictured him somehow slipping from my arms—my whole body went cold and shaky. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me on edge the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning a little. There’s always laundry, bottles to wash, texts to answer, and the baby needs me every hour. Sometimes I’ll look at the mess around me and just freeze; I don’t even know where to start. I manage to get the important stuff done, but it’s like I’m constantly playing catch-up, and I end the day exhausted and still feeling like I accomplished nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been rough. Even when the baby finally settles, my brain won’t shut off—keeps replaying everything I might’ve messed up that day. I’ll lie there staring at the ceiling, or I drift off for an hour and then jolt awake convinced I heard him cry. By morning I feel like I never really slept, just hovered in this anxious half-awake state.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, like a gray cloud that just follows me around. Sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and tears start rolling without any real reason—it’s just this constant sad, empty ache. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, but the sadness just won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I was folding his tiny onesies and just started sobbing—couldn’t even tell my husband why when he asked. It’s like the tears come out of nowhere and once they start I can’t stop them right away. I feel so silly afterward, but in the moment it feels like the only release I’ve got.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed and useless, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. ≤ 3 mo (per context)

A. Self-reported symptoms (past 7 days)
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt / self-blame over minor parenting events  
- Recurrent, intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal rumination  
- Episodic panic sensations (palpitations, breathlessness) without clear trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty unrelated solely to infant care  
- Feeling “drowning,” daily tasks “freeze” her, sense of accomplishing “nothing”

B. Endorsement pattern across EPDS-equivalent domains  
Q2-Q3-Q4-Q6-Q7-Q8-Q9: positive (≥ moderate) → depressive cluster  
Q4-Q5: positive → anxiety/panic cluster  
Q10: negative → no self-harm ideation voiced

C. Screening significance  
- Meets provisional cut-off for probable major depressive episode with anxious features; rule-out perinatal anxiety disorder  
- No safety concerns (denies self-harm)  
- Functional impairment: household task paralysis, social withdrawal, anticipatory avoidance of outings

D. Documented risk factors  
- Primiparity, sleep deprivation, perfectionistic self-expectations  
- Absence of suicidal ideation lowers acute risk; continue routine monitoring

E. Plan / next steps (screening only)  
- Recommend formal diagnostic interview (DSM-5-TR) within 1 week  
- Provide psycho-education, support resources, crisis line numbers  
- Re-screen in 2 weeks if not referred sooner
